=== Initial Brief for Mark Allan Bradbury.docx ===
SOAH DOCKET NUMBER 473-26-16349 PUC DOCKET NUMBER 59475

I, Mark Allan Bradbury (“Pro-Se Intervenor # 634”) respectfully submit this Initial Brief on behalf of myself and Heart of Texas Bowhunting, LLC.
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
I. INTRODUCTION
The issue before the Commission is not whether additional transmission infrastructure is needed in Texas. This proceeding concerns the selection of a route for one of the largest transmission projects ever proposed in Texas. While ongoing discussions exist about the necessity of the project the record demonstrates that Applicants' preferred Route 894 does not represent the route that best satisfies the statutory routing criteria established by PURA §37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §25.101.
The evidence establishes that:
Route 894 is not the shortest route.
Route 894 is not the least expensive route.
Route 894 fails to maximize utilization of existing compatible rights-of-way.
Route 894 traverses historic ranching landscapes including bisecting the Ford Ranch.
Route 894 and specifically links M12, N2, N11 and N12 traverse areas of elevated archaeological sensitivity.
Applicants failed to evaluate at least one major alternative corridor containing substantial existing transmission infrastructure.
Commission Staff determined that Route 487 possesses the greatest overall advantages and is superior to the other proposed alternative routes.
The Commission should reject Routes 392, 410, and 894 and select Route 487.

II. LEGAL STANDARD
PURA §37.056(c)(4) requires consideration of:
community values;
recreational and park areas;
historical values;
aesthetic values;
environmental integrity; and
probable improvement of service and cost.
Commission Staff witness John Poole testified that route evaluation also considers prudent avoidance, moderation of impacts on communities and landowners, and utilization of compatible rights-of-way. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 194–198
The Commission is not required to select Applicants' preferred route and may select any route supported by substantial evidence.

III. ROUTE DEVELOPMENT PROCESS DEMONSTRATES THAT FEASIBLE ALTERNATIVES EXISTED AND WERE NOT FULLY EVALUATED
Applicants have repeatedly argued that Route 894 emerged from a comprehensive routing process and therefore deserves deference. The record, however, demonstrates that Route 894 was not the only feasible route and that Applicants did not fully evaluate all constructible alternatives.
Brenda Perkins acknowledged during cross-examination that multiple route combinations identified through Requests for Information ("RFIs") were constructible but were not independently analyzed beyond the RFI process. Hearing Vol. 3 at 164.
Perkins further testified that Applicants evaluated routes on an endpoint-to-endpoint basis rather than conducting focused analysis of western corridor alternatives affecting Concho, and McCulloch Counties. Hearing Vol. 3 at 164–165.
This admission is significant. Because route scoring was performed across an approximately 220-mile project, impacts occurring within the western counties could be diluted by favorable metrics elsewhere on the route. Consequently, route evaluation may not have fully reflected the unique impacts imposed on large ranching properties, wildlife-management operations, hunting properties, and historic landscapes in the western portion of the study area.
The evidence further establishes that Applicants did not evaluate routing along the southern existing-transmission corridor discussed during Bradbury's cross-examination. Russell Marusak acknowledged that Applicants did not analyze routing along that corridor extending from Lampasas toward Big Hill East and acknowledged the existence of large transmission facilities within portions of that corridor. Hearing Vol. 3 at 139–140.
The significance of this testimony is not that the Commission must adopt the southern corridor. Rather, the testimony demonstrates that substantial opportunities for infrastructure consolidation existed and were not comprehensively evaluated.
The Commission has long recognized the importance of consolidating infrastructure into existing corridors to reduce fragmentation of rural properties and environmental resources. The record demonstrates that Route 894 does not maximize that objective.
Accordingly, the record does not support a finding that Route 894 was uniquely capable of satisfying the routing criteria.

IV. COMMUNITY VALUES FAVOR ROUTE 487
Community values are expressly identified in PURA §37.056(c)(4).
The evidence demonstrates that the character of Concho, and McCulloch Counties is fundamentally different from the urbanized eastern portion of the study area. These counties are characterized by:
• large ranching operations;
• wildlife-management properties;
• hunting leases;
• agricultural production;
• rural residential uses;
• historic ranching landscapes.
The testimony of Applicants' witnesses confirms the importance of these characteristics. Brenda Perkins acknowledged that larger ranch tracts occur west toward Big Hill and that routes may cross a single landowner more frequently than in the eastern portion of the route. Hearing Vol. 3 at 165.
Jared Gurley further confirmed that the Project's purpose is associated with the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. Hearing Vol. 3 at 146–147.
Gurley also acknowledged that Concho, and McCulloch Counties are already energized and supported by the existing electric grid. Hearing Vol. 3 at 146–147.
Thus, the western counties bear substantial routing impacts while receiving limited project-specific benefits.
The Commission has historically recognized that community values include more than population density and residence counts. Community values encompass the ways in which people use and experience the landscape. Ranching operations, wildlife management, hunting activities, and rural agricultural uses therefore constitute legitimate community values.
Route 487 better balances those values because it achieves substantially greater infrastructure consolidation while avoiding the extreme residential and cultural-resource impacts associated with Route 392 and parts of Route 894.


V. HISTORIC RANCHING LANDSCAPES AND CULTURAL RESOURCES
The record demonstrates that Route 894 traverses the Ford Ranch heritage/century landscape.
Applicant witness Russell Marusak admitted Applicants did not know the Ford Ranch was a heritage ranch during route development. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 144–145.
Historical values are an express statutory routing factor.
The testimony demonstrates that historic ranching landscapes can be affected even when no individual historic structure is removed. Visual fragmentation and introduction of major infrastructure can diminish landscape integrity and alter the historical character of a property.
The Commission may properly consider those impacts under the historical-values criterion.
The Commission should not reward incomplete historical-resource identification by approving a route that traverses a historic ranching landscape when alternatives exist.

VI. CULTURAL RESOURCES
The record demonstrates that historical resources within the study area also include recorded archaeological sites.
Staff witness Poole identified approximately 100 archaeological sites and 23 cemeteries within 1,000 feet of candidate routes. Staff Direct Testimony at 41.
Applicants identified multiple archaeological sites within the Concho–McCulloch corridor:
• 41CC331;
• 41CC350;
• 41MK47;
• 41MK48; and
• 41MN75.
These resources within route segments M12, N2, N11 and N12 occur within a broader cultural landscape extending across Concho, and McCulloch Counties.
The record further demonstrates that Route 487 crosses only two recorded cultural-resource sites and contains approximately eighteen cultural resources within 1,000 feet. Staff Direct Testimony at 41.
By contrast, Route 392 crosses approximately sixteen recorded cultural-resource sites. BCI Exhibit 61.
The cultural-resource evidence therefore provides a compelling basis for rejecting Route 392.
Route 487 traverses less high archaeological/historical-site-potential area than Route 894.

VI. ROUTE 392 SHOULD BE REJECTED
Route 392 demonstrates why no single routing criterion should control route selection.
Although Route 392 achieves substantial corridor utilization, it does so at a significant cost.
BCI Exhibit 61 shows:
• 136 habitable structures;
• sixteen cultural-resource crossings;
• 38.62 percent compatible ROW utilization.
The route therefore creates substantially greater residential and cultural-resource impacts than Route 487.
The Commission has consistently balanced corridor utilization against other statutory factors.
When all factors are considered together, Route 392 represents an overcorrection that sacrifices too much in residential and historical-resource impacts.

VII. ROUTE 410 SHOULD BE REJECTED
The evidence does not establish that Route 410 provides superior performance on any combination of statutory routing factors.
Poole's route-comparison analysis places Route 410 below Route 487 in compatible ROW/property-boundary paralleling. Staff Direct Testimony at 58.
Nor does the record demonstrate that Route 410 performs better than Route 487 on community values, historical values, environmental integrity, or cultural-resource protection.
Consequently, Route 410 provides no persuasive basis for rejecting Staff's recommended route.

VIII. ROUTE 894 SHOULD BE REJECTED
Applicants' preferred route derives much of its support from a single factor: habitable-structure count.
The evidence demonstrates that Route 894 contains approximately 85 habitable structures compared to approximately 96 for Route 487. BCI Exhibit 61.
However, Poole testified that routes such as Route 894 are longer, more expensive, and utilize less compatible ROW than Route 487. Staff Direct Testimony at 63.
JAH-12 similarly demonstrates that Route 894 leads on habitable structures but is outperformed by alternative routes on multiple other routing criteria.
The Commission's obligation is not to select the route with the fewest residences. The Commission must determine which route provides the best overall balance of all statutory factors.
The objective evidence demonstrates that Route 487—not Route 894—provides that balance.

VIII. ROUTE 487 IS THE BEST-BALANCED ROUTE
The Commission is ultimately required to balance competing routing considerations.
Route 392 overemphasizes corridor utilization.
Route 894 overemphasizes residence avoidance.
Route 410 does not demonstrate superior overall performance.
Route 487 occupies the middle ground.
It achieves:
• substantially greater corridor utilization than Route 894; BCI Exhibit 61.
• substantially fewer cultural-resource impacts than Route 392; Staff Direct Testimony at 41.
• favorable environmental performance;
• strong infrastructure consolidation;
• Staff support.
Route 487 utilizes approximately 63,000 more feet of compatible right-of-way than Route 894.
Route 487 utilizes nearly four times the amount of existing transmission-line paralleling.
These metrics directly reflect the Commission's longstanding preference for corridor consolidation and avoidance of unnecessary fragmentation.
Most importantly, Staff witness Poole concluded that Route 487 possesses the greatest overall advantages among the proposed alternatives.
The Commission should reject Routes 392, 410 and 894 and select Route 487 as it better satisfies the objectives of corridor utilization, moderation of cumulative impacts, preservation of historic landscapes, and protection of environmental integrity.


Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Mark Allan Bradbury

Mark Allan Bradbury (Pro-Se Intervenor 634)
504 Grand Avenue
Brady, TX 76825
972-742-7116
bradburyma@yahoo.com
